chunks: Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Taleqani (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id al-Hamedany, a servant of the Hashemites, said: Al-Mundhar ibn Muhammad informed us, saying: Ja'far narrated to us, from Aban al-Ahmar, who said: Al-Hussein ibn Alwan narrated to us, from Amr ibn Thabit, from his father, from Dumarah ibn Habib, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) was asked about the prayer, and he (peace be upon him) said:

The prayer is one of the principles of religion, and in it lies the pleasure of the Lord, the Exalted. It is the way of the Prophets. For the one who prays, there is the love of the angels, guidance, faith, the light of knowledge, blessing in sustenance, comfort for the body, aversion to Satan, an armor against the disbeliever, acceptance of supplication, acceptance of deeds, provision for the believer from this world to the Hereafter, an intercessor between him and the Angel of Death, companionship in his grave, a bed beneath his side, an answer for Munkar and Nakir. The prayer of the servant at the Gathering will be a crown on his head and a light on his face, a garment on his body, a veil between him and the Fire, a proof between him and the Lord, Glory be to His Majesty, a salvation for his body from the Fire, a passage over the Bridge, a key to Paradise, a dowry for the Houris, a price for Paradise. By prayer, the servant attains the highest rank, because prayer is glorification, declaration of oneness, praise, magnification, exaltation, sanctification, speech, and supplication.

key_terms.مَنْكَرٌ وَنَكِيرٌ: Munkar and Nakir (questioning angels in the grave)

ai.seo_question: What are the spiritual and eschatological benefits of prayer in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: In Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Al-Khisal*, this hadith presents prayer not merely as ritual but as a comprehensive spiritual technology that bridges the earthly and divine realms, reflecting the Shia emphasis on *Usuli* view of *salat* as the axis of faith. The text highlights the metaphysical reality of prayer as a 'crown' and 'garment' on the Day of Judgment, underscoring its role as the primary evidence (*hujjah*) between the servant and God, a concept deeply rooted in the tradition of the Ahl al-Bayt. This enumeration serves to motivate the believer by linking physical discipline with eternal reward, illustrating how the five daily prayers constitute the sustenance for the soul's journey from the world to the Hereafter.
